newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OCEANA SAYS QUOTA CUTS WILL MEAN JOB LOSSES.
newsitem.headline: OCEANA SAYS QUOTA CUTS WILL MEAN JOB LOSSES.

text.p: Efforts to reallocate fishing quotas would have to take into consideration capital investments and jobs in the formal sector, Oceana Fishing Group Ltd vice chairman Robbie Williams said on Thursday.

"The fishing industry employs a lot of people and the real concern is, if quotas are taken away from existing people, that will mean that there will be a loss of jobs because the factories can't run efficiently," he said.

There has been growing pressure for larger quotas to be granted to informal fishermen and poachers, who claim they have been denied a living because large corporations receive the bulk of fishing quotas.
But Williams said he hoped the formal sector's concerns would be taken into consideration when government drafted new policies on fishing quotas.

He earlier told the group's annual general meeting that steadily falling quotas, for natural as well as commercial reasons, had already meant that some of its facilities were operating under capacity.
"A lot depends on the resource itself. A particular problem this year is that there are just no anchovies in the sea, but they come and go," he said.

Williams said that only 400 tonnes of this year's total allowable catch (TAC) of 550 tonnes of abalone had been made available to the Quota Board for allocation to fishing companies and individual fishermen.
As a result, Tuna Marine's 1997 quota was 41 percent lower than last year but it was hoped that the position would improve when the remaining 150 tonnes were allocated.

The west coast lobster TAC for 1996/97 had been set at 1,700 tonnes, or 200 tonnes more than last year. Of this, only 1,475 tonnes had been made available, of which Oceana had been allocated 491 tonnes compared to 531 tonnes last year.
"The TAC has declined from 4,000 tonnes in 1988/89 to the current level of 1,700 tonnes," Williams said.
Catches of redeye herring, which were not limited by quotas, had started early and there had been good landings to date.
Williams said that Oceana hoped to maximise redeye herring landings this year, but it was unlikely that this would entirely compensate for the lack of anchovies.
The initial pilchard TAC was 58,000 tonnes and because the fish population seemed to be stable, this could be increased later in the year.
Quotas were expected to be allocated soon and Oceana had lobbied hard for a higher quota.
"Our vessels and cannery are able to handle substantially higher volumes of pilchard than are presently allocated, Williams said."
